Choosing a method: a side-by-side comparison

Source: vignettes/articles/method-comparison.Rmd
method-comparison.Rmd

No single integration method is best across all data regimes. MosaiClusteR gathers many methods behind one interface so you can try several on the same footing and let the evidence decide. This page is the shortcut: it lays out what each method assumes, what it accepts, and when to reach for it.

Every method takes the same input, a List of matrices over the same shared objects with objects in rows and features in columns, and returns the same {DistM, Clust} contract. So the choice below is only about behaviour, never about reformatting your data.

The five paradigms at a glance

Paradigm Idea in one line Representative functions Reach for it when
Direct Combine the sources, then cluster once ADC, ADEC You want a transparent baseline and the modalities are commensurate
Similarity-based Fuse per-source object similarities SNF, WeightedClust, WonM, NEMO Sources are noisy and complementary, at genomic scale
Graph-based Partition a graph built from many clusterings EnsembleClustering, HBGF, ClusteringAggregation You already have several base partitions to consense
Voting / consensus Let many partitions vote on co-membership M_ABC, CEC, CVAA, ConsensusClustering, EvidenceAccumulation, LinkBasedClustering You want stability under resampling, or signal hidden in feature subsets
Hierarchy-based Consense the dendrograms themselves HierarchicalEnsembleClustering, EHC The tree structure across sources is the object of interest
Factor / low-rank Cluster a shared latent representation intNMF, spectral_clustering, LUCID You want a low-rank model, or an outcome should guide the clusters

Property matrix

How to read the columns:

  • Input: data accepts raw matrices (a distance is computed internally); dist accepts a precomputed dissimilarity (type = "dist").
  • Missing a modality: whether a sample measured in only some sources can be included without imputation.
  • Reproducibility: deterministic gives the same result every run; set.seed() or a seed = argument fixes the result of a stochastic method.
  • Extra dependency: beyond base R. A dagger (†) marks an external executable (METIS) or MATLAB that is not bundled.
Method Paradigm Input Missing a modality Reproducibility Extra dependency
ADC Direct data, dist No (needs the same objects) Deterministic none
ADEC Direct data, dist No seed = none
WeightedClust Similarity data, dist No Deterministic none
SNF Similarity data No Deterministic SNFtool
WonM Similarity data, dist No Deterministic none
NEMO Similarity data Yes (averages over the omics that measured each pair) set.seed() (k-means step) none
spectral_clustering Factor affinity matrix n/a set.seed() (k-means step) none
EnsembleClustering Graph base partitions No Deterministic METIS †
HBGF Graph base partitions No set.seed() (k-means step) none
ClusteringAggregation Graph base partitions No Deterministic none
CEC Voting data, dist No Deterministic none
CVAA Voting base partitions No Deterministic none
ConsensusClustering Voting base partitions No set.seed() none
EvidenceAccumulation Voting base partitions No Deterministic none
LinkBasedClustering Voting base partitions No Deterministic (CTS, SRS); ASRS needs MATLAB † none / MATLAB †
M_ABC Voting data No seed = none (C++ kernel built in)
M_ABCdist Voting data No set.seed() none
M_ABCdeep Voting data No seed = none (self-contained R network)
HierarchicalEnsembleClustering Hierarchy data, dist No Deterministic none
EHC Hierarchy data, dist No Deterministic METIS †
intNMF Factor data (non-negative) No seed = none
LUCID Factor data plus an outcome No set.seed() LUCIDus

Two things hold for every method except NEMO: the sources must describe the same objects (MosaiClusteR aligns them by row name and tells you clearly if they do not match), and a stochastic method gives a reproducible result once you set a seed.

Data types and distances

Most methods work on continuous matrices, but the input does not have to be continuous. Distance() turns a source into a dissimilarity with a measure that suits the data:

  • continuous: "euclidean", correlation-based measures;
  • binary (fingerprints, presence or absence): "tanimoto", "jaccard", "hamming";
  • mixed-type: "gower".

Because the integration methods accept a precomputed dissimilarity (type = "dist"), you can mix data types across sources: compute a Tanimoto distance on a fingerprint source and a Euclidean distance on an expression source, then integrate the two distance matrices with the same function.

A short decision path

  1. Start with a baseline. Run ADC (or WeightedClust if you want to inspect the source trade-off). It is fast and transparent, and it gives you a reference ARI to beat.
  2. Some samples are missing a modality? Use NEMO. It is the one method here that does not need every sample in every source.
  3. Sources are noisy and complementary? Use SNF. It is the multi-omics workhorse for genomic-scale data.
  4. Want stability under resampling, or signal in feature subsets? Use the voting family, M_ABC above all, and set weighting = "nugget" for large N or heavy-tailed data.
  5. Already have several partitions to combine? Use a graph or voting consensus (EnsembleClustering, EvidenceAccumulation, CEC).
  6. The dendrogram structure is the point? Use HierarchicalEnsembleClustering.

Then compare. Extract a partition from each result with mosaic_labels(), score them with cluster_agreement(), and line them up with compare_clusterings() or ComparePlot(). The workflow is the same whichever methods you picked.

library(MosaiClusteR)
data(mosaic_toy)
L <- mosaic_toy$List

fits <- list(
  ADC  = ADC(L, distmeasure = "euclidean", normalize = FALSE),
  SNF  = SNF(L, type = "data", distmeasure = c("euclidean", "euclidean"),
             normalize = c(FALSE, FALSE), method = list(NULL, NULL)),
  MABC = M_ABC(L, NC = 3, seed = 1)
)

labs  <- lapply(fits, mosaic_labels, k = 3)
sapply(labs, cluster_agreement, b = mosaic_toy$truth)
